title: When employers do relational work: Negotiations, discounts and gift labour in the creative industries
authors: Irena Grugulis; Dimitrinka Stoyanova Russell
affiliations: Leeds University Business School, University of Leeds, UK; Cardiff Business School, Cardiff University, UK
abstract: What happens when employers engage in relational work? Relational work is work done for and with connections and kin, where motivations and rewards may stem from relational rather than market reasons. The existing literature acknowledges the workplace as a relational space but neglects employers as relational actors. Here, drawing on a qualitative study of UK film and TV production, we observe employers using relationships to discount rates and degrade working conditions. These relational markets were skewed by the asymmetries of power between employers and employees, with economic gains secured by employers and ‘immaterial’ gains allocated to employees. When employers and relationships were different, such as with charities and voluntary groups, ‘gifts’ of labour were offered. This article (a) develops our understanding of relational work by including employers as relational actors, and (b) following the relational work rationale, shows workers behaving differently depending on who their employer was.

title: Two margins of allocation and the trend in authorship inequality: Comment on Orhan, van Rossenberg, and Bal (2026)
authors: Christopher I. Rider
affiliations: Ross School of Business, University of Michigan
abstract: Abstract Orhan, van Rossenberg, and Bal (2026; hereafter ORB) report that authorship inequality in management, human resource management, and industrial-organizational psychology journals rose between 1980–1999 and 2000–2019. Their claim that “a small group of researchers has accumulated disproportionate influence over time” carries one intellectual burden, that advantage in obtaining publication opportunities increased; their interpretation of the rise as elite dominance carries a second, that the increase is inequitable. I address the first burden, on which the second depends. Because ORB compute Gini coefficients over researchers with at least one publication, they measure inequality in authorships (i.e., the intensive margin) conditional on publishing (i.e., the extensive margin), and because publication records include neither manuscript submissions nor editorial decisions, such records cannot establish that advantage increased. I demonstrate that inequality across the researchers who compete for publication opportunities rose if and only if that competing pool grew faster than field-specific thresholds of 1.2× to 2.8×, growth that publication records alone cannot substantiate. Meeting the first burden requires journal submission and decision data, which would also show whether authors differ in acceptance rates, in submissions, or in both, and so direct any intervention to its cause.

title: Individual perception of bias in grant peer review strongly associated with openness towards the introduction of lotteries
authors: Christophe Heger
affiliations: Deutsches Zentrum für Hochschul- und Wissenschaftsforschung (DZHW)
abstract: Abstract This study of a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher educa-tion institutions investigates researchers’ individual perception of bias in grant peer review and their openness towards the potential introduction of grant lotteries, as well as the poten-tial link between the two concepts. Indeed, bias in peer review is often cited in the theoretical debate on grant lotteries. But even though researchers are both very involved in and strongly affected by grant decision-making, there is not enough empirical evidence on their perspec-tive. I find that bias perception is very prevalent, openness is generally rare and researchers who perceive more bias in grant peer review are more open towards grant lotteries in a sub-stantial and statistically significant way.

title: Trended Momentum
authors: Charlie Xiaowu Cai; Peng Li; Kevin Keasey
affiliations: University of Liverpool Management School; University of Bath School of Management; University of Leeds Leeds University Business School
abstract: Abstract Drawing on cognitive psychology and behavioral theories of pattern recognition and heuristic processing, we offer a new perspective on momentum by highlighting how clear price trends shape investor expectations. Trend clarity (TC) materially strengthens momentum returns: the highest trend-clarity quintile earns annualized returns of 12.68%, compared with 6.90% for a conventional momentum strategy. We also show that TC affects momentum trading intensity within Hong and Stein’s (1999) multiperiod return-chasing model. Additional tests indicate that trading on clear trends is a central feature of momentum, distinct from existing explanations and observable across asset classes and global markets.

title: Prospect Theory and Currency Returns: Empirical Evidence
authors: Qi Xu; Roman Kozhan; Mark P. Taylor
affiliations: Zhejiang University: School of Economics and Academy of Financial Research; University of Warwick: Warwick Business School; Washington University in Saint Louis
abstract: Abstract We empirically investigate the role of prospect theory in the foreign exchange market. A currency-level measure of prospect-theory value, constructed from the historical distribution of exchange rate returns, negatively forecasts future currency excess returns. A long–short strategy based on this measure yields approximately 5% per annum. Predictability is stronger when arbitrage is limited. Bank order flow is positively associated with prospect-theory value, with inter-dealer and proprietary trading primarily driving this relation. Funds trade against prospect-theory value, acting as arbitrageurs. Overall, our findings suggest that investors evaluate currencies based on historical return distributions, consistent with prospect theory.

title: Target Firm Material Contract Redactions and Valuation in Acquisitions
authors: Paul A. Griffin; Hyun A. Hong; Kyungran Lee; Jiwoo Ryou
affiliations: University of California, Davis; University of California, Riverside; NEOMA Business School; West Virginia University
abstract: ABSTRACT We study whether and how the SEC’s confidential treatment program, which allows firms to redact proprietary information from material contracts, affects valuation in corporate acquisitions. We find that friendly acquisitions of redacting targets generate significantly higher positive announcement returns for both targets and acquirers compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. These positive returns are also more pronounced when targets are likelier to hold valuable proprietary information. In addition, friendly acquisitions of redacting targets achieve better long-term performance and recognize fewer subsequent goodwill impairments compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. Our findings of a robust association between target firm material contract redactions and target and acquirer announcement returns are consistent with a dual disclosure perspective, whereby redaction preserves target proprietary value, which is transferred privately to the acquirer through due diligence. Data Availability: Data are available from public sources identified in the paper; some require a subscription. JEL Classifications: D8; M41; M48.

title: The Limit of Nature: Thucydides and the Politics of Theory
authors: MARK D. FISHER
affiliations: Georgetown University
abstract: This article reconsiders Thucydides’s role as a foundational theorist of human nature. Contrary to conventional readings, I argue that Thucydides approaches “nature” ( physis ) less as a universal principle of behavior than as a site of political and theoretical investigation. By distinguishing his authorial voice from those of his speakers, I demonstrate that his analysis consistently approaches human nature as a limit concept—a baseline and boundary of human capacity that emerges in moments of existential precarity—while introducing a more nuanced set of terms to describe the habitual behaviors of political groups. By nevertheless foregrounding the more robust and determinative concept of nature in moments of contentious deliberation, Thucydides encourages reflection on the political dynamics that generate essentialist theories in public discourse. His account thus serves as a helpful point of reference for thinking about how competitive, polarizing speech affects the substantive categories of political debate and analysis, and through them political action.

title: How Sociotropic Aesthetic Judgments Drive Opposition to Dense Housing Development
authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN; CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF; JOSHUA L. KALLA
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley; University of California, Davis; Yale University
abstract: Voter opposition to dense housing development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize homeowner self-interest and “NIMBYism.” We develop a theory of how sociotropic aesthetic judgments shape housing policy preferences and demonstrate its unique implications with a series of descriptive studies and experiments. First, people who choose to live in dense neighborhoods have an aesthetic taste for density, leading homeowners in already-dense areas to be more supportive of dense development both in their neighborhoods and elsewhere. Second, voters are more supportive of dense development when it is proposed in already-dense neighborhoods where it “fits”—even voters who live in those same dense neighborhoods. Finally, genuine aesthetic distaste for tall buildings is widespread and causally affects support for development. Our findings offer a new lens for understanding housing policy preferences and suggest novel solutions for addressing America’s housing shortage.
